title: Fats & Oils
subtitle: 1200–300 BC · Oil, Ghee and Tallow: The Olive in Greece and Palestine, the Vedic Ghee, Sesame from the Indus to Urartu and the Fats of the Zhou

entries.label: Solon allows only olive oil to be exported from Attica
entries.hint: Plutarch’s Life of Solon says Solon’s law allowed Attica to export only olive oil of its farm produce, written on his first axon. Foxhall warns that the Solonian corpus is problematic and that scholars disagree about how much is Solon’s; the law is also hard to explain. It is nevertheless the earliest state measure on oil in the sources.
entries.note: CONTESTED (authenticity and purpose): Foxhall, Olive Cultivation in Ancient Greece (2007) ch.1 (the Solonian laws and Plutarch Life of Solon 24, citing Rhodes 2006 and Gagarin 2006; Blok & Lardinois 2006 on the corpus); Kiple, Cambridge World History of Food (2000) II.E.1 p.377 states the prohibition as fact, ‘in the early sixth century B.C.’. The date c.594 BC is the conventional date of Solon’s reforms, not given in the passages read.

entries.label: Athens protects the sacred olives: the law behind Lysias 7
entries.hint: Attica’s sacred olives (moriai) stood mostly on private land but were subject to state control and sacred to Athena, who was owed a share of their produce: the Constitution of the Athenians says the archon levied oil from the owners of plots with sacred olives and that the athlothetai measured it out to victors at the Panathenaia. Lysias’s speech 7 defends a man charged first with removing a sacred olive, then, when that was changed, with removing the enclosure where one had stood; it is the one well-documented case of private tenancy of such land, and probably peculiar.
entries.note: ANCHOR (book read): Foxhall, Olive Cultivation in Ancient Greece (2007) ch.5 §5.9 (Lysias 7; [Aristotle] Ath.Pol. 60.1–2 quoted in full) and ch.3 (on the tenancy). Foxhall says very little is known about the trees themselves; the speech is dated to the early 300s BC (c.395) by convention, not in the passage read.

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: Vedic ghee, sacred sesame and Athena’s olives

entries.label: Olive groves to keep Ra’s lamps burning
entries.hint: A papyrus has a pharaoh declare his devotion to the sun god Ra: ‘I made olive groves in your city of Heliopolis, supplied with gardeners and numerous workers charged with extracting pure Egyptian oil of the first quality, to keep alive the lamps in your sumptuous holy palace.’ Mueller adds that Egyptian pharaohs made thank-offerings of the finest olive oil to Ra and that by the Middle Kingdom Egypt produced its own oil, though Zohary judges olive horticulture ‘not a major role’ in Bronze Age Egypt.
entries.note: SECONDARY (popular history; the papyrus not read): Mueller (2011), ch.1, naming Ramses II and dating the papyrus ‘about 1000 BC’; the document usually cited for this (the Great Harris Papyrus) belongs to Ramses III, c.1150 BC — the discrepancy is unresolved here, hence the range. Zohary, Hopf & Weiss (2012) PDF p.137 (Egypt imported Levantine oil).

entries.label: Ghee, a ‘commodity of enormous prestige’, in the Vedic sacrifice
entries.hint: In the Vedic texts ghee (ghṛta), butter melted down and desiccated, was fried food, a dip, and an ingredient mixed with soma juice, and was poured on the sacrificial fire. A prayer in the Yajurveda, composed about 800 BC, asks that ‘milk, sap, ghee, honey’ prosper through the sacrifice. Cattle were so central to Vedic culture that the cow is named 700 times in the Rigveda.
entries.note: SECONDARY (Sanskrit not read): Achaya, Indian Food Tradition (1994) pp.28 (the Yajurveda prayer, PDF p.46) and 35 (ghṛta ‘a commodity of enormous prestige’, frying apūpas, mixing with soma; the cow referred to 700 times in the Rigveda; PDF p.53; OCR of a scanned PDF). Dating follows Achaya (Yajurveda c.800 BC; literature before 800 BC).

entries.label: Sesame is one of the nine sacred grains
entries.hint: From the Atharvaveda on, the Sanskrit texts mention both tila, the sesame seed, and its oil taila — a word that later came to mean any vegetable oil. Sesame was one of the nine sacred grains (navadhānya) and important in many rituals, cooked with rice and milk, made into sweets, and its oilcake compounded into fried dishes.
entries.note: SECONDARY (Sanskrit not read): Achaya (1994) p.36 (PDF p.54) — the Rigveda’s pala ‘may be the sesame’; Atharvaveda onwards tila and taila; navadhānya; tilaudana, kṛsarā, shaskuli. Compare the Harappan tila of fats-8000bc-1200bc::ec4.

entries.label: Tekoa’s oil for the Temple and the Menorah
entries.hint: Oil from Tekoa in the Judean hills was famous in Old Testament times: each year after the olive harvest it was sent in wagons to Jerusalem to be used in the Temple for ritual offerings and to light the great Menorah. The olive branch carried by Noah’s dove, Mueller adds, meant peace, since olives are slow-growing trees that can only be tended in peacetime.
entries.note: SECONDARY (journalistic account; scripture not read): Mueller (2011), the chapters on the Holy Land (the Tekoa ceremony as told to him on a visit). The date is the folio’s span for the First Temple and exile period, not a source date; see also fats-300bc-600ad::b2 on Hanukkah.

entries.label: Athena’s sacred olives and the oil of the Panathenaic prizes
entries.hint: In Attica sacred olive trees dedicated to Athena were used to make the sacred oil given as prizes in the Panathenaic games — oil literally a gift of the goddess in Athenian thought. Foxhall argues that this symbolic value, with tiny aryballoi of scented oil, hid how much of the olive crop was eaten as table olives.
entries.note: ANCHOR (book read): Foxhall (2007) ch.4 (end) and ch.5 §5.9, the Panathenaic prizes and the cultural significance of olive oil. The sacred-tree arrangements are described by Foxhall as general features of Athenian practice, so the folio dates the entry broadly to classical Athens rather than to the founding of the games.

entries.label: The Buddha allows a sick monk the fat of the fish, pig, alligator, bear and ass
entries.hint: Animal fats were used in early India and the Buddha permitted a sick monk the fats of fish, pig, alligator, bear and ass — a medical connotation, Achaya notes, since monks were otherwise bound by food rules. Together with the five medicines of the Vinaya (fats and a sweetener) it makes Buddhism’s earliest rule for the sick a list of fats.
entries.note: SECONDARY (Pali not read): Achaya, Indian Food Tradition (1994) p.37 (PDF p.55, OCR). Compare fats-300bc-600ad::b1 for the five medicines.

entries.label: The olive on the Acropolis burns in 480 BC and sprouts again
entries.hint: The Athenians guarded the ancient olive tree that Athena was said to have planted on the Acropolis and saw it as a totem of their city; when the Persians sacked Athens in 480 BC they burned it, yet green shoots soon sprang from the charred stump, reassuring the Athenians that their city would flourish again. Sophocles called the olive ‘not planted by human hands, but self-created’, and none could destroy it without divine punishment.
entries.note: SECONDARY (popular history; Herodotus 8.55 and Sophocles not read): Mueller, Extra Virginity (2011), the chapter on the Greeks (the 480 BC burning and the shoots; Sophocles’s lines on the olive watched by ‘Zeus Morios’). A legend as told, not a record.

entries.label: Anaxandrides calls the Thracians ‘butter eaters’
entries.hint: A line by the Greek comic poet Anaxandrides in the 300s BC called the Thracian enemy boutyrophagoi, ‘butter eaters’, as if eating butter proved their vulgarity. Butter had a poor reputation in the Mediterranean because the Greeks and Romans associated it with the barbarians of the north; in the south olive oil was the normal fat.
entries.note: SECONDARY (popular history; the fragment not read): Khosrova, Butter: A Rich History (2016) ch.3 (PDF p.54), ‘A line from the fourth-century play written by the Greek comic poet Anaxandrides’. Whether the line is accurately attributed or typical is not checked.

entries.label: The Zhou court’s “eight delicacies”: pig fried in melted fat, dog liver wrapped in its own fat
entries.hint: The Record of Rites, in Legge’s translation, gives the eight delicacies of the Zhou table. For the first, a sucking-pig is stuffed, coated and fried ‘in such a quantity of melted fat as to cover it’, then steamed for three days and nights. Soup balls of beef, mutton and pork mixed with rice are fried; and for the ‘Liver and Fat’ a dog’s liver is wrapped in its own fat and roasted. Fat is here the frying medium, and at the court it is animal fat.
entries.note: SECONDARY (translation read in an anthology): Legge’s 1885 translation of the Li Chi, quoted in Chang (ed.), Food in Chinese Culture (1977) p.52 (PDF p.61). The Li Chi was compiled in the Han and describes the Zhou court, so c.300 BC is the folio’s placement. Compare th2, where Needham reads the Zhou Keeper of Victuals on each meat in its own fat.

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: Herodotus’s Babylon and the fats of the Zhou li

entries.label: Herodotus: the Babylonians use only sesame oil
entries.hint: Herodotus stresses that the only oil used by the Babylonians came from sesame, not olive — a Greek traveller’s observation of the oil frontier of the Near East in the 400s BC. It fits the earlier evidence of Mesopotamian sesame cultivation (fats-8000bc-1200bc::x1).
entries.note: SECONDARY (Herodotus not read): Bedigian (ed.), Sesame: The Genus Sesamum (2011) ch.1 p.5 (PDF p.30), ‘Herodotus stressed that the only oil used by the Babylonians derived from sesame’, with her citations (Bedigian 1984, 1985, 1998, 2000, 2004a). The Herodotus passage (1.193) is not given in the text read.

entries.label: The Zhou Keeper of Victuals: each meat in its own fat
entries.hint: The Zhou li describes the Keeper of Victuals cooking each meat in its own seasonal fat: young lamb and suckling pig in beef tallow in spring, dried pheasant and fish in dog fat in summer, calf and fawn in lard in autumn, and fresh fish and goose in lamb tallow in winter. Needham notes that before the Han there is no record of pressing hemp or any other oilseed for oil: fat in ancient China was animal fat.
entries.note: SECONDARY (translation read in Needham): Needham (ed. Huang), Science and Civilisation in China 6.5, Fermentations and Food Science (2000) p.40 (PDF p.56), quoting the Zhou li (Chhun-kuan, Phao-jen) and the Li ji recipes ‘Rich Fry’; ‘very little is known about the early history of the extraction of oil from seeds in China’. The Zhou li describes a Zhou court institution but was compiled later; the entry is dated to the Warring States compilation.

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: Ekron’s presses, Athenian household consumption, Indian oilseeds, sesame oil at Karmir Blur

entries.label: Lapita cooks crack Canarium almonds and grate coconut for cream at Talepakemalai
entries.loc: Talepakemalai, Mussau Islands, and Teouma, Vanuatu
entries.hint: At the waterlogged Lapita village of Talepakemalai on Mussau, hard-shelled nuts, above all Canarium almonds, had been cracked open and thrown away by the hundreds around the stilt houses, and coconut shells, husked and cracked in half, were common in the middens; one bore on its inside the marks of a serrated shell grater. Kirch thinks the grated flesh was most likely squeezed and strained to make coconut cream, an essential ingredient of Oceanic cuisines. At Teouma in Vanuatu, where the cemetery was used about 970–800 BC, microfossils from the dental calculus of the dead show coconut, breadfruit, several nuts, bananas, taro and yams in the diet. Lapita people also carried pigs, chickens and dogs, though pig bones are few and often outnumbered by chicken.
entries.note: ANCHOR (book read): Kirch, On the Road of the Winds (rev. ed.), ch.4, PDF pp.108, 123–126, citing Tromp 2016 for the dental calculus and Petchey et al. 2015 for the Teouma dates. The coconut cream is Kirch’s ‘most likely’ inference from the grater marks; the 1000–800 BC bracket follows the later Talepakemalai phase and the Teouma cemetery.

entries.label: Oil-palm pollen surges in the Niger Delta about 850 BC
entries.hint: A soil core from the Niger Delta shows, around 850 BC, a sudden rise in oil-palm pollen and in the pollen of weeds of cultivated land, with a fall in the pollen of rain-forest trees, at a time when nothing suggests a change in climate: the palynologist M. A. Sowunmi concluded that people were opening the forest for farming, and read oil palm and yams as the main cultivars of early West African agriculture. Iron tools appear in Nigeria with the Nok culture only about 550 BC, but ground stone axes were available from 4000 BC.
entries.note: CONTESTED (interpretation) / SECONDARY: Kiple (2000) the yam chapter p.214 (PDF p.251), reporting Sowunmi 1985 pp.127–9 and Coursey. Other palynologists ask whether climate, not people, drove late-Holocene palm pollen peaks (Maley 2001, a comment whose title only was seen). The core and the date are Sowunmi’s as Kiple reports them.

entries.label: Mustard and safflower become oil sources in India
entries.hint: Mustard seed is first noticed as a source of oil in the Sutra literature after 800 BC, though the indigenous population had probably used mustard oil far earlier; the safflower is named as an oil source in early Buddhist texts. The pungent leaves of brassica were eaten as a relish (the sarson saag of today) as early as the Ācārāṅga Sūtra.
entries.note: SECONDARY (Sanskrit and Pali not read): Achaya (1994) p.36 (PDF p.54). The mustard-oil attestation follows Achaya’s dating of the Sūtra literature after 800 BC.

entries.label: Ekron’s olive-oil complex: a hundred presses
entries.hint: At Ekron (Tel Miqne) in the 600s BC excavators found more than a hundred olive-oil installations concentrated in a purpose-built industrial quarter, the largest known olive-oil production centre in the Near East of its time; Mueller adds that the mill, about 2,800 years old, had logs for lever arms and a capacity of around 500,000 litres a year. Historians read it as a deliberate economic policy under Assyrian sponsorship.
entries.note: SECONDARY (two accounts): the excavations of S. Gitin and T. Dothan as summarised in the atlas folio philistia-1200bc-604bc::ec1 (over 100 press installations, 7th century BC); Mueller, Extra Virginity (2011), ch.1 (‘a 2,800-year-old olive mill … a battery of one hundred massive presses … about 500,000 liters a year’). Mueller is a journalist and the excavation report is not in the library; the capacity is his figure.

entries.label: A sesame-oil workshop at Karmir Blur
entries.hint: At Karmir Blur on the edge of Yerevan, in the Urartian city Teishebaini, excavators found a three-room workshop for extracting sesame oil, with a storeroom of pithoi still holding oil, gutters cut in tufa to carry away waste water, and cakes of sesame; Bedigian reads it as a manufacturing centre for export in the 600s BC. Sesame has been grown in that region for three thousand years.
entries.note: SECONDARY (excavation reports not read): Bedigian (2011) ch.1 p.5 (PDF p.30), citing Piotrovskii (1950, 1952, 1969), Kassabian 1957 and Barnett & Watson 1952. Renfrew’s caution that ‘trade cannot be assumed’ is quoted there, so the export reading is Bedigian’s. Kiple (2000) II.E.4 p.413 (PDF p.450) dates the seed remains to 900–600 BC, with four large jars of carbonised sesame and ‘elaborate devices for the extraction of sesame oil’.

entries.label: Frying in ghee: the Dharma Sūtras’ vaṭakas
entries.hint: The Dharma Sūtras (600–300 BC) mention vaṭakas fried in ghee; the Rigveda’s word ghṛtavantam, ‘cooked in ghee’, for the apūpa cake suggests frying in ghee even earlier. The Aryans used only ghee for frying, Achaya says; the general populace must have used vegetable oils all along, though they first appear in the Sūtras. The Arthaśāstra has forty references to frying and names mustard oil.
entries.note: SECONDARY (Sanskrit not read): Achaya (1994) p.37 (PDF p.55, OCR). The Arthaśāstra’s date is disputed (see fats-300bc-600ad::ec5); the inference from ghṛtavantam is Achaya’s.

entries.label: Egypt burns castor oil in its lamps: Herodotus, Diodorus, Strabo and Pliny
entries.hint: Herodotus, Diodorus, Strabo and Pliny all mention Egyptians burning castor oil in lamps. Herodotus says the seeds were bruised and pressed, or roasted and boiled, to get an oil of strong smell; Strabo that the poorer people and labourers, men and women, used it to anoint the body; Pliny that in Egypt it was extracted without fire or water, the seeds being salted and pressed. Dioscorides says it was made by grinding the seeds in a mill and pressing them in baskets. Castor seeds had been in Egyptian graves since the Badarian period, and Lucas notes that Nubians still anoint with the oil.
entries.note: ANCHOR (book read, OCR of a scanned copy): Lucas, Ancient Egyptian Materials and Industries (1962) ch.XIII, ‘Castor oil’, PDF pp.399–400, summarising Herodotus, Diodorus, Strabo, Pliny and Dioscorides; the originals are not read. Egypt is filed under the Near East in the atlas. Compare fats-300bc-600ad::o1 for Ptolemy II’s tax on castor oil.

entries.label: What a wealthy Athenian household uses in a year
entries.hint: Foxhall estimates a wealthy Athenian household’s olive oil at 200–330 kg a year: 25–35 kg a person for food (about half the modern Mediterranean figure), 10–20 kg for bathing and perfume, and 90–110 kg for lighting. A symposium needs about half a litre of oil for its lamps; oil is also a mark of status in the gymnasium and at the table.
entries.note: SECONDARY (an estimate by comparison): Foxhall (2007) ch.4, Table 4.1 (p.86) and pp.91–92 — consumption for food, bathing and lighting reckoned from comparative and ancient evidence, with the author’s own cautions (‘a very crude estimate’). Not an attested figure.

entries.label: Prize oil: 1,113 amphorae for the Great Panathenaia
entries.hint: An inscription of the first half of the 300s BC records over 1,113 amphorae of oil given as prizes at the Great Panathenaia. A painted Panathenaic amphora held 38–39 litres, so some 42,000–43,400 litres were awarded — which, Foxhall reckons, would have needed the crop of about 5,500–6,500 sacred trees, if each gave 3.4–3.8 litres a harvest and two harvests plus a little off-year oil were set aside for each Panathenaia.
entries.note: ANCHOR (book read): Foxhall (2007) ch.5 §5.9, p.117, on IG I² 2311 and Shear 2003; her arithmetic on the tree yield (Neils 1992 for the amphora capacity) rests on assumptions she states. Mueller says winners also received a tax exemption on exporting the oil.

entries.label: Oil as wealth: Laconia’s revenues and Plato’s Egyptian trip
entries.hint: Oil was a vital resource in Laconia, the land of the Spartans, whose war machine Mueller says was bankrolled largely from oil revenues; Plato, the story goes, financed a journey to Egypt by selling a batch of oil, probably from his own trees. Athens and Sparta, the great rivals, were both bound up with the olive.
entries.note: SECONDARY (popular history; no ancient source named): Mueller (2011), the chapter on the Greeks. The Sparta claim and the Plato anecdote are repeated from older accounts and were not checked; Foxhall’s caution that Attica did not specialise in oil (ec8) applies.

entries.label: The unpredictable olive: why Attica did not specialise
entries.hint: Olive yields varied sharply from harvest to harvest, trees in the same region tended to bear in the same ‘on’ and ‘off’ years, and without irrigation a tree crops only every other year at best; labour needs were seasonal and clashed with the cereal sowing. For these reasons, Foxhall argues, Attic farms stayed diverse: surpluses of oil and olives were sold and sometimes exported when they came, but were neither regular nor predictable, and the main buyers of oil for a wealthy household were the household itself.
entries.note: ANCHOR (book read): Foxhall (2007) ch.3 (the unpredictability of olives; slaves as the labour of wealthy landowners) and ch.4. Her view that Attica was not an oil monoculture qualifies Kiple’s account of Solon (o1) as an oil-export policy.

entries.label: Hagnias’ thousand olive trees
entries.hint: An estate dispute over the property of a man named Hagnias, in Demosthenes 43, treats his 1,000 olive trees as an orchard large enough to be noteworthy; Foxhall reckons that 185–306 trees would cover a wealthy household’s annual oil need, little more than a well-off small farming family owned in Methana in the 1970s. Large oil estates, in other words, were not the Athenian norm.
entries.note: ANCHOR (book read): Foxhall (2007) ch.5 §5.6 and ch.6 §6.8.3, citing Demosthenes 43. The date follows the conventional date of the speech (mid-300s BC), not given in the passage.

entries.label: Sesame in a Macedonian tavern
entries.hint: Thousands of charred sesame seeds were found in a destroyed ‘tavern’ at Krania in Greek Macedonia, dated from the last quarter of the 300s BC to the first quarter of the 200s BC, among pulses, cereals, fruit, pine nuts and animal and fish bones: sesame was reaching Greek tables as the old oil frontier moved west.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Bedigian (2011) ch.1 p.5 (PDF p.30), citing Margaritis 2009. The identification of the site as a tavern and the seed as food, not oil, is the excavator’s.

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: The beam press, the oil lamp and oil as soap

entries.label: The soapstone lamp of the Arctic burns seal and whale oil
entries.hint: Oil lamps turn up at Palaeo-Eskimo sites back to the Norton tradition, some 3,000 years ago, and the soapstone lamp (the qulliq) was common to the Dorset and later Thule peoples with little change over time. It burned seal or whale oil with a wick of moss or cotton-grass, gave heat and light to winter dwellings and melted snow for water, and a piece of seal fat hung above the flame refilled it; the soapstone itself was traded over great distances. Dorset people had to accumulate enough sea-mammal oil to heat and light a winter house.
entries.note: SECONDARY (Wikipedia entries ‘Qulliq’ and ‘Dorset culture’, a Horniman Museum object entry and a Heritage Newfoundland and Labrador page, found by web search and not read in full): the ‘3,000 years’ is Wikipedia’s statement about Norton-tradition lamps, and the Dorset culture is dated there from about 500 BC. Compare fats-1000-1500::ec9 for the Thule.

entries.label: The Indian ghani, said to date from the 700s BC
entries.hint: India’s traditional oil mill, the ghani, a glorified mortar and pestle in which crushing and pressing are done in one instrument, is said to have been in use continuously since the 7th century BC for sesame, rape-mustard, coconut and castor seeds. It is, Needham notes, a design never transmitted to India’s neighbours — unlike the wedge press of China and Europe.
entries.note: SECONDARY (assertion by a scholar, not dated by a find): Needham, SCC 6.5 (2000) p.452 (PDF p.480), referring to Achaya (1993) for the ghani; the ‘seventh century BC’ is Needham’s ‘said to have been’, not an excavated date.

entries.label: The Greek beam press
entries.hint: In classical Greece, presses for both wine and oil were of the lever-and-weights, or beam, type, as shown on a black-figure skyphos in Boston and on a vase of the 500s BC; there is no evidence that the screw press was known in Greece or earlier. A pressing establishment of the 500s BC at Klazomenai shows the technology at scale. Foxhall warns that scholars often use Latin terms for Greek equipment that do not fit it exactly.
entries.note: ANCHOR (book read): Foxhall (2007) ch.6 and Figs 6.1, 6.2, 6.4 (lever press with capstan; Attic skyphos, 6th century BC, Boston 99.525; Klazomenai) with her sources (Brun 2004a: 13–17; Drachmann 1932); Needham 6.5 p.438 Fig. 94 for a beam press on a Greek vase of the 6th century BC. Page numbers beyond the figures not available in the extracted text.

entries.label: Oil and strigil: how Greeks washed without soap
entries.hint: After exercise Greek men rubbed themselves with olive oil, scented or plain, and scraped it off, the usual way of cleansing and conditioning the body; women also bathed with oil, and perfumed oil was sometimes poured into the bath water. By the Hellenistic period the oil for the town gymnasium was a regular benefaction of the wealthy. Oil, not soap, was the Greek cleanser.
entries.note: ANCHOR (book read): Foxhall (2007) ch.4 §4.3, ‘Olive oil for personal cleansing’ (Athenaios 1.24c–d for perfumed oil in the bath). Foxhall notes it is ‘difficult to estimate the quantities used’. The earliest Mesopotamian soap claim is in fats-8000bc-1200bc::te3 (unverified).

entries.label: The rotary olive crusher: Klazomenai, Greece and Israel
entries.hint: The rotary olive-crushing mill has generally been thought a latecomer, but the excavators of the 500s BC pressing site at Klazomenai suggest it preserves the earliest example; rotary crushers can be recognised in a few places in Greece by the 300s BC, though the few finds suggest limited use, and those of Israel are the next earliest. People also crushed olives by other means well into the 300s, and the rich landowners of Attica do not seem to have used rotary crushers at the end of the 400s.
entries.note: ANCHOR (book read): Foxhall (2007) ch.6 §6.4–6.5 (Klazomenai; Morel’s possible rotary grain mill of the late 500s BC; Argilos; Methana). Foxhall holds the mid-300s as the likely date of the crusher’s introduction in Attica; Klazomenai’s claim is the excavators’.

entries.label: The olive-oil lamp lights the Greek evening
entries.hint: Clay oil lamps were ubiquitous and cheap, but the oil and wick were not, so artificial light at night was a privilege of the wealthy — another form of conspicuous consumption. One small lamp burns about seven hours on 50 ml of olive oil, and a symposium needs about ten. A fragment of the comic poet Antiphanes shows the slave who set the tables also preparing the lamps.
entries.note: ANCHOR (book read): Foxhall (2007) ch.4 pp.91–92, drawing on Antiphanes in Athenaios 4.170d–e and a modern Greek lamp for the burn rate. The consumption numbers are Foxhall’s estimates (see ec2). Dalby, Food in the Ancient World (2003), ‘olive oil’, lists olive oil as fuel for lamps, soap and cosmetic.

entries.label: Who brought the olive west?
entries.loc: Greece, Italy and the western Mediterranean
entries.hint: Older scholarship credited the Greeks with bringing the olive and its oil to Italy, a view Foxhall says is still widely accepted despite evidence of olive exploitation from at least the Bronze Age. Brun suggests that olive and vine cultivation were lost to Greece after the Bronze Age and reintroduced from the Near East in the 700s BC. Zohary, Hopf & Weiss say olive cultivation was probably introduced into the western Mediterranean in the early part of the 3000s BP — about 1000 BC — by Phoenician and Greek colonists. Whether the olive spread from one centre or several remains open.
entries.note: CONTESTED: Foxhall (2007) ch.1, discussing Vallet 1962, Brun 2004a: 80–1 and Sallares 1991: 92; Zohary, Hopf & Weiss, Domestication of Plants in the Old World (2012) PDF p.138 (Boardman 1976 for the Phoenician and Greek colonists; the Uluburun shipwreck evidence is in fats-8000bc-1200bc::x4). Mueller notes domestic olives grafted on wild stock in Puglia ‘brought there by Phoenician traders and Greek colonists’.
